The final match, played at the Rose Bowl, saw England win by 6 wickets, with their batting lineup posting a competitive total and the bowlers containing the Sri Lankan attack to a modest score. The win confirmed England’s dominance in the format and reinforced their position as the world’s best side in T20 internationals.

The series, which began on 23 March, had seen England win the first two games by comfortable margins, with standout performances from key players such as Joe Root and Ben Stokes. Sri Lanka’s attempts to mount a comeback were thwarted by disciplined fielding and strategic bowling changes from the English side. With the series complete, England’s ascent to the number one ranking reflects their consistent performance across all three matches and underscores their strength in the shortest format of the game.
author: BBC Sport

title: Trump Demands Kennedy Center Recognition in Renovation Deal
content:
President Donald Trump has reiterated his demand that the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C. add his name to the institution’s official roster in exchange for his planned renovations of the historic venue.  The former president’s claim, made publicly on Friday afternoon, underscores his insistence that the Center’s recognition is a prerequisite for his proposed upgrades, which he says would preserve the building’s legacy while modernizing its facilities.

The request follows a recent court ruling that the Kennedy Center may not alter its naming conventions without a formal, legally binding agreement.  The judge’s decision, issued earlier this month, emphasized that the Center’s charter prohibits the addition of private names without a clear, public benefit and a negotiated contract.  Trump’s insistence on a name change has therefore been met with legal and institutional resistance, as the Center’s board has reiterated its commitment to maintaining its established naming policy.

The dispute highlights the broader debate over public funding and private influence in cultural institutions.  While the Kennedy Center remains open to renovations, the outcome of Trump’s demand remains uncertain, pending further negotiations and potential legal challenges.  The Center’s leadership has indicated that any future partnership will require a formal agreement that respects both the venue’s heritage and its public mission.
author: The Hill

title: Automation Displaces Specialized Professionals, Threatening Middle-Class Stability
content:
Writer John Mac Ghlionn has cautioned that the rapid adoption of automated systems across a range of industries is eroding the bargaining power of workers and displacing specialized professionals, thereby threatening the long‑term stability of the American middle class. In a recent interview, Ghlionn explained how automation reduces the need for skilled labor in fields such as manufacturing, logistics, and even certain white‑collar occupations, leaving many middle‑income workers with fewer options for upward mobility.

The writer argues that as companies increasingly rely on technology to streamline operations, traditional collective bargaining mechanisms lose leverage. With fewer skilled positions available, workers find it harder to negotiate wages and benefits, and the gap between high‑skill and low‑skill jobs widens. Ghlionn’s analysis points to a broader trend of economic polarization, where the middle class faces shrinking job security and diminishing returns on education and training.

In conclusion, John Mac Ghlionn’s warning highlights a critical challenge for policymakers and business leaders: balancing technological progress with protections that preserve the economic footing of middle‑class workers. Addressing this issue will require coordinated efforts to retrain displaced employees and to ensure that automation benefits are shared across the workforce.
author: The Hill

title: Trump Proposes New Names for AI in Truth Social Poll
content:
President Donald J. Trump used his Truth Social platform to launch a poll asking followers to choose a new name for artificial intelligence, which he described as “inaccurate.” In a Saturday post, the former president presented three alternatives—“Superior Intelligence,” “Extreme Intelligence,” and “Supreme Intelligence”—and invited his audience to vote on which label they preferred.

The poll reflects Trump’s ongoing skepticism toward the current AI terminology, a stance he has reiterated in several of his recent statements. By offering these options, he appears to be encouraging a rebranding of the technology, positioning it as a more powerful or distinct entity. The post has attracted engagement from his supporters, who have begun commenting and sharing their preferences on the platform.

The poll remains open on Truth Social, and its results will be announced once the voting period concludes. The initiative highlights the continued debate over how best to refer to and regulate emerging artificial intelligence systems.
author: The Hill

title: Congress urged to pass Goldie's Act to strengthen dog protection under Animal Welfare Act
content:
ASPCA senior vice president Nancy Perry has urged Congress to enact Goldie’s Act, a proposed bill that would strengthen enforcement of the Animal Welfare Act and protect dogs from systemic abuse. Perry highlighted the USDA’s repeated failure to enforce existing regulations, arguing that without new legal tools the agency cannot adequately safeguard animals that are routinely mistreated in shelters, breeding operations, and other facilities.

Goldie’s Act would require the USDA to conduct more frequent inspections, impose stricter penalties for violations, and expand its authority to shut down non‑compliant facilities. The ASPCA cites rising reports of dog abuse and neglect nationwide, noting that current enforcement mechanisms are too weak to deter widespread violations. Perry emphasized that the bill would provide the USDA with the resources and statutory backing needed to hold operators accountable and to ensure that the Animal Welfare Act serves its intended purpose.

In a statement to lawmakers, Perry called on Congress to act swiftly, stressing that the continued neglect of dogs under federal oversight demands immediate legislative intervention. She concluded that Goldie’s Act is a necessary step to close gaps in enforcement and to protect the welfare of dogs across the country.
author: The Hill

title: US Forces Help Transport Over 1 Billion Oil Barrels Through Hormuz Strait
content:
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) Admiral Brad Cooper announced on Saturday that U.S. forces have helped secure the passage of more than 1 billion barrels of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz in the past few months, even as the region remains in the midst of a flare‑up of strikes between Iran and U.S. forces. The Admiral said the milestone was achieved while CENTCOM assisted over 2,000 commercial ship transits in the same period, underscoring the U.S. military’s role in maintaining maritime traffic in a critical chokepoint.

The statement came amid heightened tensions following a series of retaliatory air and missile exchanges that began last month. While the U.S. has maintained a robust naval presence to protect shipping lanes, the Admiral highlighted that the continued flow of oil has not been disrupted by the hostilities. He noted that the U.S. has worked closely with commercial shipping companies and regional partners to coordinate safe passage and mitigate any operational risks.

CENTCOM’s efforts are part of a broader strategy to preserve the free flow of global energy supplies, a priority for both U.S. and allied interests. The Admiral’s remarks reaffirm the U.S. commitment to maritime security in the Persian Gulf, even as diplomatic efforts seek to de‑escalate the conflict with Iran.
author: The Hill

title: Malaria elimination needs multiple tools, expert says
content:
Malaria cases and deaths have climbed globally, a trend highlighted in a new review by George Washington University global health expert Nirbhay Kumar. The study points to rising drug resistance and the diminishing efficacy of insecticide‑treated bed nets as key obstacles to current control efforts. Kumar notes that the World Health Organization’s latest surveillance data show an increase in confirmed cases across sub‑Saharan Africa and parts of Southeast Asia, underscoring the urgency of a more robust response.

Kumar argues that eliminating malaria will require a multifaceted approach rather than reliance on a single intervention. He calls for the accelerated deployment of next‑generation antimalarial drugs, the integration of novel vaccines such as RTS,S with existing prevention tools, and the development of new vector‑control strategies that address insecticide resistance. The review stresses that coordinated investment in research, surveillance, and community‑based programs is essential to sustain gains and prevent further setbacks.

In conclusion, the review warns that without a diversified strategy, the global malaria burden is likely to continue rising. Policymakers and international partners are urged to adopt an integrated framework that combines proven interventions with innovative solutions, ensuring that progress toward malaria elimination remains on track.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Australia Launches Dynamic Ice Sheet Modeling Workflow
content:
Ice sheets are critical components of the Earth system, with Antarctica and Greenland representing the only two major continental ice masses on the planet. Their sheer size and mass make them key regulators of global processes, and changes to these ice sheets can reverberate far beyond their immediate surroundings.

The dynamics of the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets directly affect global sea‑level rise, ocean circulation, and atmospheric patterns. Melting ice contributes to rising sea levels, while the influx of fresh water into the oceans can alter thermohaline circulation, influencing climate zones and weather patterns across mid‑latitude regions. Additionally, the albedo effect of the ice surfaces modulates the amount of solar radiation reflected back into space, thereby impacting regional and global temperature regimes. The stability of these ice sheets also has societal implications, as rising seas threaten coastal communities and infrastructure, and changes in ocean currents can influence fisheries and maritime navigation.

Given their broad influence on climate, weather, and human societies, continuous monitoring and research of Antarctica and Greenland are essential for predicting future environmental changes and informing global adaptation strategies.
author: Phys.org

title: Nullarbor Plain: Australia's Largest Limestone Region
content:
The Nullarbor Plain, stretching more than 200,000 square kilometres (77,000 square miles) across southern Australia, is one of the planet’s largest limestone regions. The flat, treeless expanse lies between the Great Australian Bight and the Southern Ocean, forming a continuous limestone plateau that dominates the landscape of South Australia, Western Australia, and the Northern Territory.

Geologists explain that the plain originated when a shallow sea that once covered the area receded about 14 million years ago during the Miocene epoch. As the sea withdrew, the underlying limestone was exposed and subsequently eroded, leaving behind the stark, featureless terrain that characterises the Nullarbor today. The region’s geological history has attracted scientific interest, and its unique environment supports a range of specialised flora and fauna adapted to the arid conditions.

The Nullarbor remains a significant natural landmark for both scientific research and tourism. Its vast, limestone‑rich landscape continues to be studied for insights into ancient marine environments and the processes that shape large-scale karst landscapes worldwide.
author: Phys.org

title: Avoid Using AI for Substantive Writing
content:
A recent Substack post titled “Why you should almost never use AI” has sparked discussion among the tech community. The author argues that generative AI systems, while impressive, are fundamentally unreliable for tasks that demand accuracy, accountability, or nuanced judgment. The piece highlights several risks: the tendency of models to hallucinate facts, the difficulty of tracing responsibility when outputs are produced, and the potential for AI to reinforce existing biases when trained on large, unfiltered datasets.

The article cites specific examples, such as AI-generated code that contains subtle bugs, medical advice that can be dangerously inaccurate, and creative writing that often reproduces copyrighted material without proper attribution. It also points out that current AI tools lack transparent provenance, making it hard for users to verify the source of information or to correct errors. On Hacker News, commenters largely echoed these concerns, noting that while AI can accelerate routine work, it can also spread misinformation if used indiscriminately. Some users suggested that the solution lies in better oversight and clearer guidelines for AI deployment rather than outright avoidance.

In conclusion, the Substack post and the ensuing Hacker News thread underscore a growing caution in the tech sector: AI should be employed sparingly and with rigorous safeguards. The debate highlights the need for clearer standards around AI transparency, error handling, and ethical use, especially as the technology becomes more integrated into everyday workflows.
author: Hacker News

title: Supabase Announces Hiring for OrioleDB Positions
content:
Supabase, the open‑source alternative to Firebase, has recently posted a new position focused on its Orioledb database technology. The job listing appears on the company’s careers page and was shared on Hacker News under item 49768220, where it has yet to receive any upvotes or comments.

The role, titled “Orioledb Engineer,” calls for experience with PostgreSQL‑compatible storage engines, performance tuning, and distributed database design. Candidates are expected to work closely with the core Supabase team to extend Orioledb’s feature set, improve scalability, and contribute to the open‑source community. The position is remote‑first, with no specified location, and applicants can submit their résumé and cover letter through Supabase’s online application portal.

At present, the Hacker News post has not attracted any engagement, indicating that the announcement is still fresh. Prospective applicants are encouraged to review the full job description on Supabase’s website and apply directly if they meet the qualifications.
author: Hacker News

title: Substack article examines why knowledgeable people often sound uncertain
content:
A Substack essay titled “The People Who Know the Most—Often” has drawn attention on the technology news aggregator Hacker News, where it currently holds 24 points and has generated seven comments. The piece, authored by writer and researcher Vrash, examines the social and cognitive dynamics that lead certain individuals to become frequent sources of information across a range of topics. By analysing anecdotal evidence, historical examples, and recent research on expertise and information networks, the author argues that a combination of curiosity, interdisciplinary exposure, and active community engagement tends to concentrate knowledge in a relatively small group of people who are repeatedly consulted for advice.

Readers on Hacker News have responded with a mix of appreciation for the essay’s synthesis of psychological literature and skepticism about its broader applicability. Commenters note that while the article highlights the value of “knowledge hubs” in fostering rapid problem‑solving, it also raises concerns about over‑reliance on a limited pool of voices, potentially marginalizing alternative perspectives. The discussion underscores ongoing debates about how expertise is recognized and disseminated in digital communities, especially as platforms increasingly surface content based on popularity metrics rather than depth of insight.

Overall, the Substack post has sparked a concise yet substantive dialogue about the mechanisms that elevate certain individuals to the status of go‑to knowledge sources. The conversation reflects broader interest in understanding how information authority is constructed online, suggesting that future research may focus on balancing the benefits of trusted experts with the need for diverse, inclusive input in collaborative environments.
author: Hacker News

title: Trump Bans CNN, MS Now, Politico from White House
content:
President Donald Trump warned that CNN, MSNBC and Politico would be barred from the White House, a claim that turned out to be more than a headline.  According to NPR, the three outlets were physically turned away from the White House this morning, marking a new escalation in the administration’s approach to media access.  The move follows a directive that was issued while Chief of Staff Susie Wiles was out of town, a fact that many senior White House officials reportedly found surprising.

Politico, which had been seeking clarification, noted that the decision was made abruptly and without prior consultation with senior staff.  The ban is being viewed by observers as part of a broader pattern of the administration’s efforts to limit coverage by outlets critical of the president, raising concerns about potential First Amendment implications.  The White House has yet to issue a formal statement explaining the rationale behind the directive.

In the wake of the incident, media organizations are monitoring the situation closely, while legal experts weigh the possible constitutional ramifications.  The incident underscores the heightened tensions between the Trump administration and the press, and it remains to be seen whether the ban will be upheld or reversed in the coming days.
author: The Verge

title: Navy CTO Justin Fanelli Urges Co-Investing with VCs, Highlights $562M Refueling Deal
content:
The U.S. Navy’s Chief Technology Officer, Justin Fanelli, announced a strategic shift in how the service engages with emerging technology. Rather than directly funding early‑stage research, the Navy will now partner with venture capital firms to co‑invest in promising startups, allowing the Department to tap into private expertise while sharing risk and reward. Fanelli said the new model would accelerate the adoption of breakthrough solutions and streamline the procurement pipeline.

In a recent showcase of the Navy’s new approach, the service completed a $562 million purchase of an autonomous refueling system that can transfer fuel to ships without human intervention. The deal, one of the largest of its kind, demonstrates the Navy’s commitment to integrating unmanned capabilities into its fleet. Alongside this acquisition, Fanelli outlined an updated wish list for future innovations, prioritizing advances in artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and other high‑impact technologies that could reshape naval operations.

The Navy’s updated strategy signals a broader effort to stay ahead of emerging threats while fostering a robust ecosystem of defense entrepreneurs. By co‑investing with venture capital partners and targeting next‑generation technologies, the Department aims to secure a competitive edge and maintain operational readiness in an increasingly complex security environment.
author: TechCrunch

title: Google says Gemini AI model stopped hacks promptly
content:
Google announced that its Gemini platform acted appropriately by terminating each hacking attempt immediately, following a series of security incidents reported over the past month. Gemini, Google’s advanced AI system designed to enhance data protection and threat detection, identified and halted unauthorized access attempts on several internal and external services before any data could be exfiltrated.

According to a statement from Google’s security team, the platform’s real‑time monitoring algorithms flagged anomalous activity, triggered automated containment protocols, and logged the events for forensic analysis. The company confirmed that no user data was compromised and that the incidents were isolated to specific test environments. Google said it will continue to refine Gemini’s threat‑response capabilities and will conduct a full audit of its security posture.

The company reiterated its commitment to protecting user information and maintaining robust defenses against cyber threats. Google will keep stakeholders informed of any further developments and plans to strengthen its AI‑driven security infrastructure.
author: TechCrunch

title: Black Smoke Rises Near Riyadh Airport as Flights Cancelled
content:
Flames and plumes of smoke were seen rising near Riyadh airport this afternoon, forcing the cancellation and delay of several flights. The incident comes amid intensified fighting between Saudi‑backed government forces and Iran‑backed Houthi rebels, which has already claimed 48 lives in recent hours.  

The Houthi rebels launched a rapid offensive this month, seizing large swaths of territory in Yemen and mounting a barrage of missiles and drones aimed at Saudi Arabia. The escalation has disrupted air traffic in the capital, prompting authorities to ground aircraft for safety reasons while they assess the damage and secure the airport perimeter.  

The incident underscores the growing volatility in the region and the broader implications of the Yemen conflict for Saudi Arabia’s security and aviation operations. Authorities continue to monitor the situation closely as the conflict unfolds.
author: France 24

title: Macron visits Saint Pierre and Miquelon, first French presidential visit in over a decade
content:
President Emmanuel Macron departed Paris on Saturday for a three‑day trip to Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a small French archipelago off Newfoundland with a population of fewer than 6,000. The visit marks the first time a French head of state has set foot on the islands in more than a decade. Macron will meet Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, underscoring the close ties between the two North‑Atlantic partners amid growing diplomatic friction with Washington.

Saint Pierre and Miquelon remain France’s sole remaining possession in North America, a vestige of the country’s colonial reach. The islands have long served as a symbolic reminder of France’s overseas presence, and Macron’s itinerary includes a review of local defense cooperation and a discussion of economic development with Canadian officials. The timing of the trip coincides with heightened tensions between Paris and Washington over trade and security issues, prompting observers to view the visit as a strategic gesture of solidarity with Canada.

The trip is expected to reinforce Franco‑Canadian relations and signal France’s continued commitment to its overseas territories. While the islands are small, the visit carries symbolic weight, reminding the world that France still maintains a foothold in North America and that it remains engaged in Atlantic affairs.
author: France 24

title: Germany prepares for Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state elections as AfD seeks gains
content:
Germany is preparing for two crucial state elections on Sunday, with voters in the capital Berlin and the predominantly rural state of Mecklenburg‑Western Pomerania set to cast their ballots. The far‑right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is the focal point of the contests after achieving its strongest showing to date in the recent Saxony‑Anhalt elections, a result that has heightened expectations that the party could make further inroads in both regions. The elections are being closely watched as a barometer of the AfD’s expanding appeal and as a test of the governing coalition’s ability to contain the party’s anti‑immigration platform.

The outcomes are expected to pose a significant challenge for Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose leadership is under scrutiny as the AfD’s surge threatens to reshape the political landscape in key German states. Analysts note that a strong performance by the AfD could compel the Chancellor’s party to reassess its strategy ahead of upcoming national contests, while a setback for the far‑right would reaffirm the current government’s standing. The results on Sunday will therefore provide a decisive indicator of the AfD’s momentum and its impact on Germany’s broader political dynamics.
author: France 24

title: UN Crime Congress examines technology's impact on crime and law enforcement
content:
Monica Juma, the United Nations Deputy Secretary‑General, spent the morning in her Vienna office reviewing briefing papers ahead of a high‑level United Nations gathering in Abu Dhabi. The summit, convened by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, will bring together ministers, law‑enforcement leaders and civil‑society representatives to assess the rapid transformation of criminal activity and to chart a coordinated response. Juma emphasized that the pace of change in organized crime, cyber‑enabled fraud and illicit finance now outstrips the capacity of many national and international institutions that were designed for a pre‑digital era.

The Abu Dhabi meeting is expected to focus on strengthening legal frameworks, enhancing cross‑border data sharing and expanding resources for capacity‑building in vulnerable jurisdictions. Delegates will discuss proposals for a new global treaty on cybercrime, reforms to the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, and mechanisms to better protect victims of trafficking and illicit exploitation. Juma’s remarks underscored the urgency of modernising governance structures, noting that without swift adaptation the gap between criminal innovation and institutional response could widen, undermining global security and development goals.
author: UN News

title: UN General Assembly remains key forum for global issues
content:
More than eight decades after its inaugural session in 1946, the United Nations General Assembly continues to serve as the principal forum where all 193 Member States convene to address the world’s most pressing issues. Convened each year in New York, the Assembly provides a platform for diplomatic dialogue on a broad spectrum of topics, ranging from conflict resolution and peacekeeping to sustainable development, climate action, and the protection of human rights.

The enduring relevance of the General Assembly lies in its inclusive structure, which allows every member nation an equal voice in shaping the international agenda. As global challenges evolve, the Assembly’s debates and resolutions remain central to coordinating multilateral responses, reinforcing the United Nations’ mandate to promote peace, prosperity, and universal rights for all peoples.
author: UN News

title: Global efforts to strengthen pandemic preparedness continue
content:
Six years after COVID‑19 claimed millions of lives, strained health systems and halted global commerce, policymakers and health experts remain focused on strengthening pandemic preparedness. The World Health Organization’s 2023 review highlighted persistent gaps in disease surveillance, vaccine manufacturing capacity, and equitable distribution mechanisms, noting that many low‑ and middle‑income countries still lack the infrastructure to detect and respond to emerging pathogens swiftly. In response, the G20 health summit in early 2024 pledged an additional $50 billion to a new Global Pandemic Fund, earmarked for expanding genomic sequencing networks, bolstering supply‑chain resilience for personal protective equipment, and supporting rapid‑response research platforms that can accelerate vaccine development within weeks of an outbreak.

Despite these commitments, recent assessments indicate that funding disbursements have been uneven and that national pandemic plans often remain outdated. The United Nations Development Programme reported that only 38 % of the targeted nations have completed a comprehensive review of their health emergency strategies, and the International Monetary Fund warned that the economic shock from future pandemics could exceed the $10 trillion loss experienced during COVID‑19 if preparedness gaps persist. As governments negotiate the next round of health security legislation, the emphasis is shifting toward integrated data sharing, cross‑border coordination, and sustained investment in public‑health workforce capacity to ensure a more coordinated global response to any future health crisis.
author: UN News

title: Thousands protest Kennedy Center closure after board vote
content:
Thousands of demonstrators gathered on the steps of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on Saturday for the “Hands Around the Kennedy Center” rally, protesting a decision by the venue’s board of trustees to shutter the iconic cultural institution. The board, whose members were appointed by the Trump administration, voted earlier this week to close the Center, citing financial deficits and a proposed restructuring plan that would eliminate several performance spaces and reduce staff. Organizers of the rally, including local arts nonprofits and community leaders, formed a human chain around the building and delivered a petition demanding the board reverse its decision and explore alternative funding solutions.

The protest comes amid growing criticism of the board’s handling of the Center’s budget and concerns that the closure would deprive Washington, D.C., of a major platform for theater, music, and dance. City officials have not yet responded to the petition, while the Kennedy Center’s management indicated that the vote was intended to prompt a broader dialogue with stakeholders. As the debate continues, supporters of the venue pledge to maintain pressure on the trustees, emphasizing the Center’s historic role in American arts and its impact on the local economy.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Brighton defeat Arsenal 3-0 as Manchester City rise to Premier League lead
content:
Arsenal’s title challenge suffered a setback on Saturday when they were beaten 3‑0 by Brighton & Hove Albion at the Falmer Stadium, a result that handed Manchester City the Premier League lead on goal difference. The Gunners, who entered the match as league leaders, were unable to recover after conceding early, and the visitors’ three‑goal margin left Arsenal three points behind City, who remain unbeaten in their own fixtures.

The defeat drops Arsenal to second place while City, with a superior goal‑difference tally, move to the summit of the table. Both clubs remain on 71 points, but the six‑goal swing in the Brighton game widens the gap, intensifying the race for the title as the season approaches its climax.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Ed Sheeran to Perform Solo After Musicians Quit Tour Over Macklemore Gaza Expulsion
content:
Ed Sheeran is considering performing solo after several supporting musicians withdrew from his upcoming tour, following the recent expulsion of rapper Macklemore from the same lineup. The departures were prompted by Macklemore’s public statements in support of Palestine, which led organizers to remove him from the roster. In response, a number of accompanying artists announced they would no longer participate, citing concerns over artistic freedom and the handling of political expression.

Tour promoters confirmed that the show will proceed, with Sheeran prepared to fill the vacant slots himself. The incident has sparked broader debate within the music industry about the limits of political commentary and the repercussions for performers who address contentious issues. Organizers indicated that ticket sales and dates remain unchanged, and fans can expect the scheduled performances to continue as planned.
author: Al Jazeera

title: White House denies access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters
content:
Reporters from CNN, MSNBC and Politico were denied entry to the White House on Saturday, preventing them from covering a scheduled presidential event. The denial affected the news organizations’ ability to file stories from the premises, and the journalists were turned away at the security checkpoint without being provided a specific reason for the restriction.

A White House spokesperson said the decision was based on “operational constraints” related to the event’s limited capacity and security protocols, emphasizing that the administration continues to accommodate the press corps in accordance with established guidelines. The three outlets issued brief statements expressing disappointment and noting the importance of unfettered access for transparent reporting. The incident adds to ongoing discussions about press access to the executive branch, though officials indicated that future briefings would proceed with the usual media attendance.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Dutch police disperse far‑right protest in The Hague
content:
The justice minister publicly condemned the display of Nazi‑style salutes, antisemitic chants and violent incidents that occurred during an anti‑immigration rally held in the capital on Saturday. In a statement released to the press, the minister described the behavior as “unacceptable and contrary to the values of a democratic society,” and pledged that law‑enforcement agencies would pursue all individuals involved in unlawful conduct.

Police reported that several participants were detained after clashes erupted between rally attendees and counter‑protesters, and that investigators are reviewing footage of the extremist symbols and slogans for possible prosecution. The minister’s remarks come amid heightened scrutiny of far‑right groups in the country, with authorities emphasizing their commitment to uphold constitutional protections and to prevent hate‑motivated violence.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Cuba restores power after sixth nationwide blackout this year
content:
An electricity outage struck the capital city early Tuesday, marking at least the sixth disruption of its power grid this year. Utility officials confirmed that the blackout affected residential neighborhoods, commercial districts and several government facilities, prompting emergency crews to restore service while urging citizens to conserve energy until normal operations resumed.

The series of outages follows the implementation of a United States‑imposed energy blockade that took effect earlier in the year, restricting the import of fuel and related equipment. Analysts note that the blockade has constrained the nation’s ability to maintain its power infrastructure, leading to recurring supply shortfalls and heightened vulnerability of the grid during peak demand periods. Authorities have reiterated their commitment to mitigating the impact on the population while seeking alternative sources to stabilize the energy system.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israel conducts airstrikes on Nabatieh, hits ambulance team
content:
Two Israeli air strikes struck the southern Lebanese city of Nabatieh in quick succession, followed moments later by a third strike that hit an ambulance team operating in the area. The attacks were reported by local authorities and confirmed by on‑the‑ground witnesses, who said the first two explosions hit residential neighborhoods while the third targeted a medical vehicle responding to the initial blasts.

Lebanese officials said the strikes caused damage to several buildings and resulted in injuries among civilians and emergency responders, though the exact casualty figures have not yet been released. The Ministry of Health condemned the targeting of the ambulance, describing it as a violation of international humanitarian law, while the Lebanese military announced that it was monitoring the situation and would investigate the incident. Israeli military spokespeople did not immediately comment on the specific operations.

The incident adds to a series of cross‑border confrontations that have escalated in recent weeks, underscoring the heightened tension between Israel and groups operating in southern Lebanon. Both sides have called for restraint, and international observers are watching the developments closely as they could influence broader regional stability.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Iran Sends Conditions for Talks to US via Qatar, Awaits Trump Reply
content:
Tehran – Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera that Iranian officials are awaiting a response from former U.S. President Donald Trump on a pending diplomatic matter. Rezaei said the Iranian side has submitted its position and is now expecting a reply that could shape the next steps in the dialogue between the two nations.

The Iranian statement comes amid ongoing discussions about regional security and potential economic sanctions, topics that have featured prominently in recent U.S.–Iran interactions. While no specific details were disclosed, Rezaei emphasized that a timely answer from the United States would be essential for Iran to determine its subsequent diplomatic and strategic actions. The waiting period underscores the cautious approach both sides are taking as they navigate complex bilateral issues.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Converse withdraws Instagram ad after backlash over KKK imagery
content:
Social media users have criticized a recent post from a brand’s Instagram account, claiming that the image shared resembled a Ku‑Ku‑Klan hood and a hanging. The visual, which was circulated widely on platforms such as Twitter and TikTok, prompted a surge of comments labeling the content as racially insensitive and offensive. Users highlighted the similarity between the dark, pointed hood depicted in the photograph and the historic attire associated with the white supremacist organization, while also noting that the composition evoked imagery of a noose.

The brand has not yet issued an official statement addressing the allegations, and the post remains under scrutiny as the conversation continues online. Observers note that the incident underscores ongoing concerns about cultural awareness and the potential impact of visual branding on public perception. The controversy may prompt the company to review its social‑media practices and consider corrective measures to mitigate reputational damage.
author: BBC World

title: White House takes press badges from CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters
content:
White House officials confiscated the press credentials of reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, the three outlets confirmed on Tuesday. The badges were taken during a routine credential check after the journalists attempted to cover a scheduled briefing, according to statements released by the news organizations. The White House press office did not immediately provide a comment on the specific reasons for the seizure.

The incident has prompted concerns among media groups about access to the executive branch, with the affected outlets emphasizing the importance of unrestricted reporting from the nation's capital. The White House has historically maintained a credentialing system for journalists, and any removal of badges is typically reserved for violations of its policies. The three news organizations said they are seeking clarification and will pursue appropriate steps to restore their reporters’ access to the White House press pool.
author: BBC World

title: Houthi rebels claim attack after smoke seen near Riyadh airport, flights disrupted
content:
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh experienced a significant incident on Tuesday that forced the temporary closure of several runways and led to hours of flight disruptions across the kingdom’s busiest hub. Airport officials reported that all inbound and outbound commercial flights were halted for approximately six hours while security teams investigated the source of the disturbance and cleared the affected areas. The shutdown affected more than 150 scheduled departures and arrivals, prompting airlines to rebook passengers and divert some flights to alternative Saudi airports.

The disruption occurred against the backdrop of heightened tensions in the region, as Saudi Arabia intensifies its military campaign against Houthi rebels in Yemen. Recent weeks have seen an increase in cross‑border attacks, including missile and drone strikes targeting Saudi infrastructure. While authorities have not confirmed a direct link between the airport incident and the ongoing conflict, the timing underscores the broader security challenges facing the kingdom’s aviation network amid the escalating war. Normal operations at King Khalid International Airport resumed by late evening, and officials continue to monitor the situation for any further threats.
author: BBC World

title: Aston Villa grab victory despite late Spurs goals as De Zerbi’s side are booed off
content:
Aston Villa secured their first Premier League victory of the season with a 3–2 win over Tottenham Hotspur, ending the Spurs’ campaign in the most disappointing fashion. The hosts took advantage of first‑half added time to claim the lead while Tottenham were temporarily reduced to ten men, a situation that left the visitors vulnerable. Villa’s second‑half performance was characterised by a tight defensive structure and swift counter‑attacks, with Nicolas Jackson and Emi Buendía each finding the net. Johan Manzambi added a third goal for the Gunners, but the late consolation was not enough to halt the defeat.

Spurs’ loss marks the worst start to a Premier League campaign in the club’s history, and the two late goals underscore the team’s struggle to convert early momentum into results. Despite the setback, the match offered glimpses of progress for Unai Emery’s side. The defensive solidity displayed in the second half and the clinical finishing from the counter‑attack suggest that the Spanish manager’s “turbo‑charged” rebuild is beginning to take shape. The result, however, will force Tottenham to address their defensive frailties and find a more consistent approach if they are to avoid further humiliations in the months ahead.
author: Guardian Sport

title: England beat Sri Lanka by eight wickets in T20
content:
At 2:30 pm BST the England team’s match against Sri Lanka was in its second over, with the score at 22‑0.  The innings opened with a solid start from Nissanka, who had already taken eleven wickets, and Udara, who had claimed ten.  Archer’s first two deliveries were cut away on the off‑side by Udara, while Jofra’s wide ball was followed by a top‑edge hook from Nissanka that sailed for a six, giving the Sri Lankan bowlers a quick advantage.  England’s batting line‑up was still finding its rhythm, with JimA’s top‑edge and Buttler struggling to maintain control of the gloves.

Meanwhile, outside the field, it was announced that Carse will not face any charges, a decision that has been welcomed by the team’s management.  The commentary team, including Read the Spin, highlighted the early pressure on England, noting that the TV camera focused on key bowlers such as Fleming, McCullum and Southee as they set the boundary.  The collective noun for New Zealand teams, “Kiwis,” was also mentioned in a lighter segment of the broadcast.

With the scoreboard still at 22‑0, England will look to regroup and accelerate their run rate in the coming overs.  The match will continue to unfold with the Sri Lankan bowlers maintaining their early dominance, while England’s batsmen will aim to break the initial lull and establish a more competitive position.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Emery praises Jackson and Suzuki after Villa's 3-2 win over Spurs
content:
Aston Villa secured a hard‑won 3‑2 victory at Tottenham Hotspur, a result that has bolstered their position in the Premier League standings. The match, played at the Spurs’ home ground, saw Villa overcome a resilient Tottenham side to claim three points in a tightly contested encounter.

Manager Unai Emery praised his squad’s determination, noting the team’s resilience as a key factor in the win. He singled out striker Nicolas Jackson for his decisive contribution, which included a crucial goal, and goalkeeper Zion Suzuki for a series of impressive saves that helped preserve the lead. Emery highlighted how both players exemplified the club’s fighting spirit throughout the match.

The victory reinforces Villa’s campaign momentum and demonstrates their capacity to compete against top‑flight opposition. With the win, the club continues to build confidence as the Premier League season progresses.
author: BBC Sport

title: Goodwin Double Leads London City to First Away Win
content:
London City Lionesses secured their first away win of the season in a convincing victory over Charlton Athletic, a team that has lost all three of its current Women's Super League fixtures. The match, played at Charlton’s home ground, saw the Lionesses dominate the game and finish with a comfortable win.

Isobel Goodwin was the standout performer, finding the net twice to give the Lionesses a decisive advantage. Her brace helped the team to a clear win, while Charlton’s attack failed to register any points, extending their winless streak to three games. The result leaves the Lionesses with a morale‑boosting away triumph, whereas Charlton remain in a precarious position at the bottom of the table.

With this victory, London City Lionesses now have a positive away record for the season and can look forward to building on the momentum. Charlton Athletic, meanwhile, must address the issues that have led to their current slump as the league continues to unfold.
author: BBC Sport

title: De Zerbi urges Tottenham to show more blood and fight after Villa defeat
content:
Tottenham Hotspur suffered a defeat to Aston Villa in their recent Premier League fixture, prompting head coach Roberto de Zerbi to call for a stronger performance from his squad. De Zerbi said that the team’s behaviour on the pitch was more important than the raw quality of the players, noting that the club must improve its collective discipline and decision‑making if it is to compete at the highest level.

The loss highlighted a pattern of inconsistency for Spurs, who have struggled to maintain momentum in recent matches. De Zerbi’s comments come as the club seeks to address issues of concentration and tactical execution, both of which were evident in the defeat. He emphasized that the team’s attitude and work ethic would need to be elevated to match the standards expected in the Premier League.

Looking ahead, Tottenham will focus on tightening their defensive structure and improving communication among players in training sessions. The club’s management and coaching staff remain committed to making the necessary adjustments to regain form and secure better results in the remainder of the season.
author: BBC Sport

title: Tottenham Lose to Aston Villa, No Revival in Sight
content:
Tottenham Hotspur suffered another setback at the Emirates Stadium, falling 3‑1 to Aston Villa in a Premier League fixture that further deepened the club’s recent slump. Villa’s early goal from a well‑placed header set the tone, and a second from a long‑range strike forced the visitors to double up on the defense. Spurs were unable to find a breakthrough, with their lone goal coming from a late penalty that proved insufficient to alter the outcome. The defeat left Tottenham in the bottom half of the table, five points adrift of safety.

The loss underscores the team’s ongoing struggles to convert chances into points. Despite a solid start, Tottenham’s midfield failed to maintain possession, and the attack was hampered by a lack of creativity and finishing. Manager Ange Robinson admitted the squad needs to regain confidence and cohesion, citing the need for better defensive organization and sharper clinical work in front of goal. Villa’s manager praised his side’s disciplined approach, noting that the win was a result of disciplined defending and efficient counter‑attacks.

With the Premier League still in its early stages, Tottenham’s position remains precarious. The defeat adds to a series of disappointing results that have left the club’s supporters frustrated, and it highlights the urgency for the team to address both defensive frailties and offensive inefficiencies if they are to avoid a relegation‑danger zone. The club will look to rebound in their next fixtures, hoping to halt the downward trend and stabilize their campaign.
author: BBC Sport

title: Man Utd Muslim Supporters Club calls for Sir Jim Ratcliffe's resignation
content:
The Manchester United Muslim Supporters Club has demanded that co‑owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe step down following remarks he made in which he criticised immigration policy and described the United Kingdom as “on the slide.” The club, which represents a significant portion of the team’s fan base, said Ratcliffe’s comments were “unacceptable” and “contrary to the values of the club and the wider community.”  

Ratcliffe’s statements were made in a recent interview with a national media outlet, where he warned that unchecked immigration could undermine the country’s social fabric. The club’s statement emphasised that the club has long championed diversity and inclusion, and that such remarks are at odds with the club’s public commitments to those principles. The club also called on United’s board to consider the impact of the owner’s views on the club’s reputation and its relationship with fans.  

In response, United’s board has yet to issue an official statement. The club’s call for Ratcliffe’s resignation reflects growing pressure from supporters and community groups for the ownership to align its public conduct with the values it promotes on and off the pitch.
author: BBC Sport

title: Canada Hold England to 26-26 Draw at Sandy Park
content:
England’s impressive winning streak was halted when the national side drew 26‑26 with Canada at Sandy Park. The match, played in front of a packed home crowd, saw both teams trade goals in a high‑scoring affair that kept spectators on the edge of their seats until the final whistle.

England entered the game on a run of consecutive victories, having won their last ten fixtures across friendlies and competitive matches. The draw came after a late equaliser from Canada, which forced the match into a stalemate at 26‑26. Key moments included England’s early lead, a series of counter‑attacks that saw Canada level the score, and a tense finish that saw neither side secure a win.

With the draw, England’s unbeaten run comes to an end, marking a rare setback for the team in the lead‑up to the upcoming tournament. The result will prompt a reassessment of tactics ahead of England’s next fixtures, while Canada can take confidence from the hard‑fought draw against a traditionally stronger opponent.
author: BBC Sport

title: Trump Bans CNN, MS NOW, Politico From White House; Reporters Denied Access
content:
A day after President Donald J. Trump announced that he would bar reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, all three outlets confirmed that their journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. Trump’s statement followed accusations that the outlets had published “purposefully negative stories” about his administration. The decision to restrict coverage came amid a broader pattern of heightened scrutiny and criticism of the press by the former president.

The White House spokesperson said the ban applied to the three outlets’ reporters, but did not specify whether it extended to other media. The outlets, in turn, reported that their journalists were turned away at the gates and were unable to attend any briefings or events. The move has drawn attention from media watchdogs and press‑freedom advocates, who note that the ban follows a series of confrontations between the Trump administration and the press over coverage of policy and political developments.

While the White House has not yet issued a formal statement detailing the duration or scope of the ban, the incident underscores the tense relationship between the former president’s administration and mainstream media. The outlets have indicated that they will continue to cover the White House through alternative means, and the situation remains under close observation by journalists and observers of press freedom.
author: The Hill

title: Trump Administration Targets Foreign Journalists with New Visa Policy
content:
The United Kingdom has announced a new visa‑compliance framework that will tighten the conditions under which foreign journalists can enter and remain in the country. The policy, unveiled by the Home Office on Tuesday, expands the scope of background checks and requires media organisations to provide detailed disclosures about their editorial policies and funding sources. The government says the changes are intended to safeguard national security and prevent the spread of disinformation.

The new rules mirror similar measures used by Russia, China and Iran, where visa restrictions have been employed to punish reporters and outlets that publish unfavorable coverage of the state. Under the UK proposal, journalists who are found to have disseminated content deemed “inconsistent with the public interest” could face visa revocation or denial of future applications. Press freedom groups have warned that the policy could create a chilling effect on investigative reporting and reduce the presence of independent media in the UK.

While the Home Office maintains that the reforms are a routine update to existing immigration procedures, critics argue that the expanded powers could be used to target dissenting voices. The policy is set to take effect in the coming months, and its impact on foreign media operations will be closely monitored by both domestic and international observers.
author: The Hill

title: White House Denies Access to CNN, MS NOW, Politico Journalists
content:
The White House denied journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico access to its grounds on Saturday, a day after President Donald Trump announced a ban on the networks following accusations that they were producing “purposefully negative stories.” The ban came after the president publicly criticized the outlets for their coverage of his administration, prompting a formal statement from the White House that the journalists would not be allowed onto the premises.

According to the networks, MS NOW reporters were specifically turned away early in the morning, while CNN and Politico staffers were also prevented from entering the compound. The White House reiterated that the decision was made in response to the president’s directive and that no alternative arrangements were offered. The incident follows a broader pattern of tensions between the administration and the press, with the president’s remarks underscoring his frustration with what he perceives as hostile coverage.

The denial of access highlights ongoing disputes over media coverage and presidential authority. While the networks have not yet announced any further actions, the situation underscores the heightened scrutiny and conflict surrounding the administration’s relationship with the press.
author: The Hill

title: Politicians Shield Against Press Coverage
content:
This week, a series of actions by political leaders underscored a growing trend of shielding themselves from critical coverage. Reports indicate that officials from both parties are increasingly using their offices and official resources to limit access for journalists who publish unfavorable stories, citing concerns about public safety and the integrity of the press. The measures include restricting press briefings, controlling media access to certain events, and employing staff to manage the flow of information to reporters.

President Donald Trump has taken a more overt stance by issuing an executive order that bans the dissemination of what he describes as “critical media” content. The order, which has sparked debate over its constitutionality, specifically targets outlets that the administration claims spread misinformation or undermine national security. While the administration frames the ban as a protective measure for the public, critics argue that it infringes on First Amendment rights and could set a dangerous precedent for press freedom.

The developments highlight a tension between the principle of a free press and the perceived need for governmental control over information. As lawmakers and the executive branch continue to enact measures that restrict media access, the broader implications for transparency and democratic accountability remain a key concern for observers and legal experts alike.
author: The Hill

title: 1970s Baby Names Still Common Among 50‑Year‑Olds
content:
A recent analysis of Social Security name data indicates that adults in their fifties are highly likely to bear one of the three most popular first names from the 1970s. The study, which examined birth records from 1970 to 1979, found that names such as Michael, Jennifer, and David accounted for more than 70 % of male and female births that decade, and that roughly 80 % of people born during those years still carry those names today. The researchers noted that the concentration of these names in the 50‑plus age group reflects the strong cultural influence of the era, from television and film to popular music.

The trend is consistent across both genders, with male names like James, John, and Robert also showing high retention rates among those now in their fifties. Analysts point out that naming patterns tend to cluster around a few culturally resonant choices, and that the 1970s saw a surge in traditional, biblical, and Anglo‑saxon names. This clustering effect means that a significant proportion of the current 50‑plus population shares a common set of first names, making them more recognizable and easier to identify in demographic studies.

These findings underscore how naming conventions can serve as a demographic marker for specific age cohorts. While newer generations continue to diversify their naming choices, the legacy of the 1970s persists, offering researchers a clear lens through which to examine generational identity and cultural continuity.
author: The Hill

title: State Department Approves $2.6B Air Defense Sale to Ukraine
content:
The U.S. State Department announced on Friday that it has approved a potential $2.6 billion sale of air‑defense equipment to Ukraine, following a resumption of hostilities with Russia after recent trilateral talks with U.S. special envoys. The notification to Congress lists a range of systems that the Ukrainian government has requested, including S‑300 clone surface‑to‑air missiles, GAM‑67 missiles, range‑extended air‑defense laser‑guided rocket missile systems, and counter‑drone platforms.

The approval reflects Washington’s continued effort to strengthen Ukraine’s defensive capabilities against Russian air and missile threats. By providing advanced air‑defense technology, the United States aims to enhance Ukraine’s ability to protect critical infrastructure and deter further escalation. The sale is part of a broader package of military assistance that has been expanded in response to the renewed conflict on the eastern front.
author: The Hill

title: Civics students identify classmates as major obstacle to participation
content:
A recent survey of high‑school and college students found that a striking 91 percent of those who admitted to self‑censoring cited classmates as the primary source of concern. The study, conducted by the Institute for Youth Communication at State University, surveyed 1,200 students across five states and asked respondents to identify the groups or individuals that most influenced their decision to withhold opinions or feelings in school settings.

Respondents reported that peer pressure, fear of ridicule, and the desire to maintain social harmony were the main drivers behind their self‑censorship. The data also revealed that students in larger schools and those participating in competitive extracurricular activities were more likely to report classmates as a significant influence. Researchers noted that the high percentage underscores the pervasive role of peer dynamics in shaping student expression and highlighted the need for schools to foster environments that encourage open dialogue.

The findings suggest that educators and policymakers should consider targeted interventions—such as peer‑mentoring programs and inclusive classroom practices—to mitigate the pressure that leads students to silence themselves. By addressing the social factors identified in the study, schools may help create safer spaces where students feel comfortable sharing diverse perspectives.
author: The Hill

title: FAA mandates eternal flame on Trump arch to warn pilots
content:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a statement on Saturday indicating that President Donald Trump’s proposed Triumphal Arch in Washington, D.C., would need a permanent “eternal flame” at its summit to serve as a warning to pilots operating in the surrounding airspace. The agency’s determination specifies that the arch must be marked with a non‑standard flame and that floodlight projectors be positioned to illuminate the structure for visibility during night operations.

The FAA’s conditions arise from concerns about the arch’s proximity to the National Mall and the potential for the monument to interfere with aviation safety. By requiring a conspicuous flame and directed lighting, the agency aims to ensure that the arch is easily identifiable from the air and does not pose a hazard to aircraft. The proposal, which has been under discussion for several years, would see the arch erected on a prominent site in the capital, prompting the FAA to review its impact on flight paths and air traffic control.

In summary, the FAA’s latest guidance mandates specific safety features for the Triumphal Arch, underscoring the importance of clear visual markers for nearby pilots. The agency’s decision reflects ongoing efforts to balance commemorative projects with the operational requirements of the national airspace system.
author: The Hill

title: Three reporters denied White House entry after Trump ban
content:
Three reporters were denied entry to the White House grounds Saturday morning, a day after President Donald Trump announced that CNN, Politico and MS NOW would be barred from the premises for publishing what he described as “fiction and lies.” The three journalists, whose affiliations were not disclosed, arrived for scheduled interviews but were stopped at the security checkpoint and escorted out without being granted access to the press briefing area.

The incident follows the president’s escalating criticism of major news outlets, which has raised concerns among media organizations about the administration’s approach to press freedom. White House officials declined to comment on the specific reasons for the blockage, citing standard security protocols, while the White House press office reiterated that all accredited reporters are subject to the same entry requirements. The episode underscores ongoing tensions between the Trump administration and the news media, highlighting the delicate balance between security measures and the public’s right to information.
author: NPR Politics

title: Lib Dems target record 73 MPs in snap election, says Davey
content:
Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, has announced that the party intends to surpass its 2024 record of 72 seats in any forthcoming snap election. The statement was made during a press briefing in which Davey outlined the party’s strategy for capitalising on a potential early general election, noting that the current parliamentary strength reflects a significant recovery from the 2017 and 2019 defeats.

The 72‑seat tally, achieved in the 2024 general election, marked the highest number of MPs the Liberal Democrats have held since the 1980s. Davey emphasised that the party’s policy platform—focused on climate action, public services, and electoral reform—has resonated with voters, and that the party is preparing to expand its presence in key marginal constituencies. He also highlighted the importance of a coordinated campaign to maintain momentum should an early election be called.

In concluding remarks, Davey reiterated the party’s commitment to a robust electoral campaign and urged supporters to engage in grassroots mobilisation. He added that the Liberal Democrats will continue to monitor the political landscape and adjust their approach to maximise gains in any snap election scenario.
author: BBC Politics

title: White Matter Bundles Connect Brain Hierarchy to Mental Functions
content:
Recent research has highlighted the critical role of white matter in coordinating the brain’s complex functions. Scientists emphasize that movement, perception, memory, reasoning, emotion, and many other cognitive processes depend on seamless communication between distinct brain regions. White matter, composed mainly of insulated nerve‑cell fibers, serves as the highway that carries these signals across the brain.

The insulated fibers, or axons, in white matter enable rapid and efficient transmission of neural impulses. By linking disparate cortical and subcortical areas, white matter supports the integration of sensory input, motor planning, and emotional regulation. Disruptions in white‑matter integrity have been associated with a range of neurological and psychiatric conditions, underscoring its importance in maintaining healthy brain function.

Understanding the mechanisms of white‑matter communication offers promising avenues for therapeutic interventions. Advances in imaging and neurobiological techniques may soon allow clinicians to detect early white‑matter changes, potentially guiding treatments aimed at preserving or restoring connectivity in disorders that impair cognition and behavior.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Florida reports dengue death amid worst outbreak in decades
content:
Florida is grappling with one of the most severe dengue fever outbreaks in decades, with the latest data from the Florida Department of Health indicating a sharp rise in confirmed cases across several counties. The state’s public health officials report that the surge has now resulted in a fatality, marking the first death linked to the disease in Florida since the early 2000s. The outbreak follows a pattern of increasing dengue activity in the southeastern United States, driven in part by warmer temperatures and expanded mosquito breeding habitats.

According to the department’s weekly epidemiological bulletin, more than 1,200 cases have been confirmed statewide, with the majority concentrated in the Miami‑Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach counties. Health authorities attribute the spike to the presence of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the primary vector for dengue, which thrives in the region’s humid climate and urban environments. In response, the Florida Department of Health has intensified mosquito control efforts, deployed larvicides, and launched a public awareness campaign urging residents to eliminate standing water and use protective measures such as screens and repellents. Hospitals in affected areas have increased their capacity for dengue testing and treatment, and the state has coordinated with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for additional resources.

The fatal case underscores the seriousness of dengue’s potential complications, including hemorrhagic fever and organ failure, especially in vulnerable populations. While the disease remains relatively rare in Florida, the current outbreak highlights the need for vigilant surveillance and community engagement to curb transmission. Public health officials continue to monitor the situation closely and advise residents to seek medical attention promptly if they experience fever, severe headache, or joint pain—symptoms that could signal dengue infection.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Argentina's Suicide Rates Reach Historic Highs
content:
Argentina’s suicide rate has climbed to its highest level in two decades, prompting a growing movement of bereaved families and mental‑health professionals to open a national conversation on the issue.  In recent months, several survivors of suicide loss have spoken publicly about the gaps in support and the stigma that often surrounds mental‑health challenges, urging the public and policymakers to address the crisis with greater urgency.

Data from the Ministry of Health show that the annual number of suicides rose from 3,200 in 2018 to 4,100 in 2023, with the most significant increases among young adults aged 18 to 34.  In response, a coalition of psychologists, psychiatrists and grief‑support groups has launched a media campaign and a series of town‑hall meetings across major cities, aiming to normalize discussions about depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation.  The coalition also recommends expanding crisis‑intervention services, integrating mental‑health education into school curricula, and providing training for primary‑care providers to identify at‑risk patients.

The initiative has already drawn attention from several provincial health ministries, which are reviewing funding proposals for expanded outreach programs.  While the conversation remains in its early stages, the coordinated effort of bereaved relatives and mental‑health specialists signals a shift toward greater public engagement and a potential re‑evaluation of Argentina’s approach to suicide prevention.
author: Medical Xpress

title: West African labs urge governments to boost outbreak detection as health systems weaken
content:
West African laboratory scientists urged governments on Friday to boost outbreak‑detection capacity, warning that regional health systems are becoming increasingly fragile. The call, issued by a coalition of national virology and microbiology labs, came amid growing concerns that weak surveillance could allow a new epidemic to spread unchecked.

Scientists highlighted gaps in sample‑transport logistics, diagnostic equipment, and trained personnel, noting that recent outbreaks of Lassa fever and sporadic Ebola cases have exposed the limits of current infrastructure. They urged ministries of health to allocate additional funding for rapid‑test kits, expand laboratory networks, and strengthen data‑sharing protocols with international partners such as the World Health Organization.

The coalition’s message stresses that timely detection is the first line of defense against disease spread. By investing in laboratory capacity now, West African governments can prevent the recurrence of large‑scale outbreaks and safeguard the region’s public health gains.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Student assessment overhaul could boost well‑being
content:
A recent survey of secondary‑school students asked, “When you were in school, what stressed you out the most?” The results showed that classroom assessments—graded tests, quizzes, group projects, presentations, and laboratory work—ranked as the primary source of anxiety for the majority of respondents. According to the study, 68 % of participants identified at least one type of assessment as a significant stressor, with written exams and oral presentations cited most frequently.

The data also revealed that students in higher‑level courses reported greater anxiety, with 74 % of those in advanced placement or honors classes citing assessments as a major concern. Educational researchers note that the pressure to perform well on these graded activities can affect mental well‑being and academic performance. The survey’s authors recommend that schools consider diversified assessment strategies, such as formative feedback and portfolio work, to mitigate stress while maintaining rigorous standards.

These findings underscore the need for educators and policymakers to balance assessment demands with student well‑being. By exploring alternative evaluation methods and providing targeted support, schools may reduce assessment‑related anxiety and foster a healthier learning environment.
author: Phys.org

title: San Rock Art Dinosaur Claims Debunked by Researchers
content:
For years, paleontologists have entertained the notion that the San and Basotho peoples of southern Africa had long recognized dinosaur fossils, weaving them into oral traditions, songs, and cave art. Proponents of the theory point to purported carvings and legends that seem to describe large, extinct reptiles, suggesting that these communities possessed an early awareness of prehistoric life. The idea has gained traction in popular science circles, framing indigenous knowledge as a valuable, often overlooked source of paleontological insight.

Recent investigations, however, have called the evidence into question. Scholars specializing in African archaeology and anthropology have examined the cited cave paintings and oral accounts, finding that many of the images can be reinterpreted as depictions of contemporary fauna or symbolic motifs rather than literal fossil representations. Linguistic analyses of the associated myths also reveal that the terminology used does not align with known descriptions of dinosaur anatomy. In addition, the supposed fossil sites cited by earlier researchers have been re‑evaluated, with many lacking the stratigraphic context required to confirm the presence of dinosaur remains.

The emerging consensus is that while the San and Basotho cultures possess rich mythological traditions, the claim that they consciously identified dinosaur fossils remains unsupported by the available archaeological and linguistic data. As a result, the hypothesis is being treated with caution, and researchers are urged to rely on more robust, multidisciplinary evidence when exploring the intersections of indigenous knowledge and paleontology.
author: Phys.org

title: Humpback Whale Spotted in Sacramento River 60 Miles from Pacific Ocean
content:
Denny Glover, a local angler, was on a routine fishing outing with friends along the Sacramento River when an unexpected sighting turned the day into a headline. While casting lines in hopes of a sizable catch, Glover spotted a fully grown humpback whale drifting near the river’s banks. The whale, estimated to be over 50 feet long, appeared disoriented and was soon surrounded by onlookers and nearby boaters.

River authorities were alerted immediately and dispatched a team of marine biologists and rescue specialists. The whale was assessed for injuries and health, and a temporary containment plan was implemented to keep it safe while transport arrangements were made. The incident has prompted a review of river navigation protocols and raised questions about the presence of large marine mammals in inland waterways during certain seasons. The whale is expected to be transferred to a rehabilitation center for further evaluation.
author: Phys.org

title: New Wild Cat Species Discovered in Bolivia Sanctuary
content:
A team of biologists has formally identified a previously unknown cat species in plain sight at a wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia. The small, spotted feline, which has lived unnoticed for years among the sanctuary’s resident fauna, was recognized as a distinct taxon after a detailed morphological and genetic analysis conducted by researchers from the University of La Paz and the International Cat Conservation Society.

The new species, tentatively named *Felis boliviensis*, measures roughly 30 centimetres in body length and displays a unique pattern of dark spots on a sandy‑brown coat, a feature that has allowed it to blend into the forest floor. DNA sequencing of mitochondrial genes confirmed that it is not a variant of any known South American wild cat, but rather a separate lineage within the *Felis* genus. The discovery underscores the biodiversity hidden in protected areas and highlights the importance of ongoing monitoring and research in the region.

Conservationists say the identification of *Felis boliviensis* will prompt a review of the sanctuary’s management plans to ensure the species’ habitat is preserved. The researchers plan to conduct further ecological studies to determine its population size, diet, and reproductive habits, with the goal of integrating the species into national wildlife protection policies.
author: Phys.org

title: Narwhals Used to Monitor Arctic Warming
content:
The Arctic is gaining an unlikely champion in the fight against climate change: the narwhal. Recent studies show that these iconic, spiral‑tusked cetaceans help regulate the ocean’s carbon cycle by transporting carbon from the surface to deeper waters through their feeding and excretion patterns. As they dive for Arctic cod and other prey, narwhals facilitate the sequestration of carbon, a process that can slow the rate of atmospheric warming in the region.

Scientists have linked narwhal migration routes to key carbon‑rich zones, noting that their presence coincides with increased sedimentation of organic matter on the seafloor. The animals’ seasonal calving and breeding cycles also influence local nutrient dynamics, supporting phytoplankton growth that absorbs carbon dioxide. With Arctic sea ice shrinking, protecting narwhal habitats could become a critical component of broader climate mitigation strategies, as the species’ health reflects the overall resilience of the marine ecosystem.

Conservation efforts are now focusing on reducing shipping traffic, limiting oil and gas exploration, and monitoring narwhal populations to safeguard this natural carbon sink. By preserving the narwhal’s role in the Arctic’s carbon budget, policymakers and researchers hope to strengthen the region’s capacity to buffer global climate change, underscoring the interconnectedness of marine life and planetary health.
author: Phys.org

title: ORNL releases LandScan Mosaic dataset mapping daily building use
content:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), a laboratory of the U.S. Department of Energy, has unveiled LandScan Mosaic, a next‑generation global population distribution dataset. Building on the foundation of ORNL’s widely used LandScan Global, the new product incorporates dynamic modeling of building usage and occupancy patterns to estimate where people are located throughout the day.

LandScan Mosaic refines population estimates by integrating data on building types, usage schedules, and occupancy rates, producing a more temporally accurate picture of human presence. The enhanced resolution and temporal granularity are expected to benefit a range of applications, from improving disaster response and humanitarian assistance to informing infrastructure planning and national security operations worldwide.

The release of LandScan Mosaic represents a significant step forward in spatial analytics, offering stakeholders a more precise tool for decision‑making in critical sectors. As the dataset becomes available to researchers and planners, its adoption is likely to enhance the effectiveness of global efforts to manage risk, allocate resources, and protect communities.
author: Phys.org

title: Tin: Full‑Text Search Engine for PostgreSQL
content: PlanetScale today unveiled Tin, a new data‑warehouse offering that lets developers run analytical queries on the same data that powers their applications without moving it to a separate system. Built on the company’s existing Vitess
author: Hacker News

title: Zig: A Rust-Inspired Language with a Different Safety Model
content:
